Chapter 13
Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery, And One's Own

Auxiliary troops are the other useless type of military force. You use them when you call on a powerful ally to bring his army to help and defend you. Pope Julius the Second did exactly this in recent times. During his campaign against Ferrara, he saw firsthand how pathetic his mercenary troops were. So, he turned to auxiliaries and made a deal with King Ferdinand of Spain to supply him with soldiers and weapons. These auxiliary forces might be capable and effective on their own, but they are always a disaster for the ruler who invites them in. If they lose, you are ruined. If they win, you become their prisoner.

And although ancient history is full of examples, I want to stick with this recent case of Pope Julius the Second. The danger of his decision is obvious. To capture Ferrara, he threw himself completely into the hands of a foreign power. But good fortune intervened and caused a third, unexpected event, saving him from the consequences of his reckless choice. His auxiliary troops were crushed at Ravenna. However, Swiss troops then rose up and drove out the conquerors, surprising everyone, including the Pope. As a result, he avoided becoming a prisoner of his enemies, because they ran away. He also avoided becoming a prisoner of his auxiliaries, because he ultimately won the war using different troops.
The Florentines, having no army of their own, sent ten thousand French soldiers to conquer Pisa. By doing this, they put themselves in greater danger than at any other time during their struggles.

The Emperor of Constantinople wanted to push back his neighbors, so he brought ten thousand Turkish soldiers into Greece. When the war was over, the Turks refused to leave. This disastrous decision was the beginning of Greece's enslavement by the infidels.

Therefore, any ruler who wants to guarantee he will not win should use these troops. They are far more dangerous than mercenaries. With auxiliaries, your ruin is guaranteed from the start. They operate as a unified force, and they obey someone else. Mercenaries, on the other hand, need more time and a better opportunity to turn against you after a victory. They are not a single, united organization. You recruited them, and you pay them. Even if you appoint a commander to lead them, that commander cannot seize enough power quickly enough to destroy you. In short, the greatest danger with mercenaries is their cowardice. The greatest danger with auxiliaries is their competence. Therefore, a wise prince always avoids these foreign armies and relies entirely on his own troops. He would rather lose with his own men than win with someone else's. He knows that a victory won with foreign armies is not a real victory at all.

I will never hesitate to highlight Cesare Borgia and his actions. The Duke invaded the Romagna region using auxiliary troops. His entire army consisted of French soldiers, and with them, he captured Imola and Forli. But he quickly realized these forces were not reliable. He switched to mercenaries, thinking they were less dangerous, and hired the Orsini and Vitelli factions. When he actually put them to work, he found them to be disloyal, unreliable, and highly dangerous. So, he wiped them out and finally turned to his own men. You can easily see the difference between these types of armies by looking at the Duke's reputation. Notice how he was viewed when he used the French, when he used the Orsini and Vitelli, and finally, when he relied completely on his own soldiers. Once he had troops whose loyalty he could count on, his power and prestige grew relentlessly. He was never respected more highly than when everyone saw he was the absolute master of his own forces.

I intended to stick to recent Italian examples, but I must include Hiero of Syracuse, since I mentioned him earlier. As I noted, the Syracusans made him the commander of their army. He quickly recognized that their mercenary troops, organized much like our modern Italian condottieri, were completely useless. He realized he could not safely keep them, nor could he simply let them go. So, he had them all hacked to pieces. From that day on, he fought his wars using his own troops, never relying on foreigners.

I also want to remind you of a story from the Old Testament that fits this perfectly. David offered to fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, on behalf of King Saul. To give David courage, Saul armed him with his own royal weapons. But as soon as David put the armor on, he rejected it. He told the king he could not fight properly with someone else's gear, and he chose to face the enemy with only his sling and his knife. The lesson is simple: the armor of others will either fall off your back, weigh you down, or bind you tight.

Charles the Seventh, the father of King Louis the Eleventh, used his own ability and good fortune to liberate France from the English. He understood that he desperately needed to be armed with his own forces, so he established a permanent system of cavalry and infantry in his kingdom. Later, his son, King Louis, abolished the national infantry and started hiring Swiss mercenaries instead. This massive mistake, followed by others, is exactly why the French kingdom is in peril today. By elevating the reputation of the Swiss, he ruined the value of his own military. He destroyed his infantry completely. He also subordinated his own cavalry to foreign mercenaries. Because his cavalry became so used to fighting alongside the Swiss, they now believe they cannot win without them. As a result, the French cannot defeat the Swiss, and without the Swiss, the French cannot defeat anyone else. The French army has become a mixed force, part mercenary and part national. This mixed army is much better than using only mercenaries or only auxiliaries, but it is vastly inferior to relying entirely on your own troops. This example proves the point perfectly: the kingdom of France would be completely unconquerable if they had simply maintained or expanded the military system created by Charles.

But the limited wisdom of men often leads them to start something that looks good at first, blinding them to the poison hidden underneath. This is just like the hidden fevers I mentioned earlier. Therefore, a prince who cannot recognize a deadly problem until it is already upon him is not truly wise. Unfortunately, this kind of insight is rare. If you look at the first disaster that struck the Roman Empire, you will find it started the moment they began hiring Goths into their army. From that day forward, the strength of the Roman Empire began to collapse, and all the incredible power they once held was drained away and handed to foreigners.

I conclude, therefore, that no state is secure unless it has its own military forces. Without them, you are entirely dependent on fortune, because you lack the strength and ability to defend yourself when adversity strikes. Wise men have always judged that nothing is as fragile and unstable as a reputation for power that is not backed by your own strength. Your own forces are armies made up of your subjects, your citizens, or your dependents. Everything else is either a mercenary or an auxiliary. The method for building your own army is easy to find if you study the rules I have laid out. Look closely at how Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, and many other successful republics and princes armed and organized themselves. I fully commit myself to their example.
